acquisition.why: Buyers come inbound through eBay or Amazon search. Agents can draft listings and set prices from sold-comps data. This depends fully on the platform.

onboarding.why: Marketplace checkout needs no customer onboarding. Sourcing does: bidding on lots (UK equivalents such as police or public-sector auction houses [E]) needs a human to judge condition, value and collection.

delivery.why: Physical work every time: collect lots, store, inspect, photograph, pack and ship. A 3PL at small-lot volume would erase the margin [E].

billing.why: Marketplace payments are automatic. Fee and VAT tracking can be automated.

support.why: Agents can answer routine eBay messages. Returns, damaged items and disputes need a human to handle the goods.

scores.R_why: £300 can buy small UK lots [E], but each lot is a gamble on mixed condition. He would also need storage and collection trips, which are hard with a toddler and 6-8 h/week. Batteries and electricals bring WEEE, battery and product-safety obligations. The examples are US-centric (GovDeals); the £45k Google Glass example is far beyond budget.
scores.M_why: Arbitrage reselling on eBay is crowded and margins are thin. Edge comes from sourcing luck rather than anything defensible. AI does not commoditise it, but it doesn't help scale it either.
scores.one_line: A hands-on, capital-gambling arbitrage with second-hand anecdotes ('pennies to $10') and no first-hand proof; physical handling makes it unsuitable for an agent-run business.

acquisition.why: Paid social and Amazon listings can be agent-managed for ad variants and bids, with human approval of spend and claims. ASA/CMA rules on fake UGC need a human compliance check.

delivery.why: Co-manufacturer plus FBA or a 3PL can run without him day to day. Formulation, testing, MOQs and inventory decisions need human work.

billing.why: Shopify or Amazon payments are automated.

support.why: Questions about health, adverse reactions and product quality need human judgement and carry liability.

scores.R_why: Private-label gummy MOQs typically run into thousands of pounds [E], far above £300. UK food-supplement labelling, permitted health claims (GB NHC register), FSA and ASA rules apply, and supplements carry product-liability risk. He has no supplement expertise.
scores.M_why: Creatine and greens gummies are heavily saturated on Amazon UK. Big brands outspend on ads, and AI-generated ad creative lowers the barrier for everyone.
scores.one_line: The '$1M/month' example is explicitly hypothetical and the Grüns figures are guesses; this is capital-heavy, regulated, saturated physical ecommerce that doesn't fit a £300 agent-run test.

acquisition.why: Players could come via SEO. Supply is the problem: owners are private individuals, so PECR blocks cold messaging them, and listing their courts without permission is a privacy and trust problem. Supply acquisition needs human outreach.

onboarding.why: Owners need verification, access rules and insurance arrangements set up per property.

delivery.why: Software can handle booking, but physical access, no-shows, damage and safety need human handling.

billing.why: Stripe Connect-style split payments can be automated [E].

support.why: Disputes between strangers on private property need a human.

scores.R_why: Private home sport courts are rare in the UK, including Bromley [E]. UK pickleball play runs through leisure centres and clubs that already have booking systems (e.g. Playtomic, ClubSpark [E]). Building a two-sided marketplace in 6-8 h/week is unrealistic.
scores.M_why: UK supply is tiny and incumbent court-booking platforms cover public courts. Liquidity at local scale is unlikely.
scores.one_line: A single-video hypothetical with no traction claims; UK has almost no private-court supply and PECR blocks the 'list first, contact owners' tactic.

acquisition.why: Meta ads and Amazon can be agent-optimised with human approval of spend. This depends on paid platforms.

delivery.why: Sugar is hand-packed in a garage and shipped. A co-packer or 3PL is possible, but shipping a heavy, low-value product is uneconomic.

support.why: Agents can handle routine queries. Shipping problems and quality complaints (mould) need a human.

scores.R_why: Hummingbirds do not live in the UK, so there is effectively no domestic demand. Even selling into the US from the UK, a heavy sugar product cannot survive international shipping costs.
scores.M_why: There is no UK market. The nearest UK analogue, wild-bird food, is dominated by established brands and retailers [E].
scores.one_line: These are genuine first-hand US results (repeat buyers, Meta ads) but the product is irrelevant to the UK; the only lesson that transfers is the QR-code reorder loop.

acquisition.why: SEO articles, YouTube and lead magnets are inbound and legal, and agents can draft them. Building an audience takes months to years and needs credible expertise.

onboarding.why: Course or community platforms such as Mighty Networks handle signup and access unattended.

delivery.why: Recorded courses need an expert to film and maintain them. Animal-care content cannot safely be AI-only.

support.why: The membership's value is herd-specific expert answers and live calls, which are human every time.

scores.R_why: Ricardo has no goat, smallholding or mushroom expertise. The model depends on years of trusted content: Deborah had a 2,000-person list and six months of build-up. UK smallholding guidance differs on breeds, parasites, vets and Defra/APHA rules. A UK mushroom-growing variant is more feasible but still needs hands-on content [E].
scores.M_why: There are established UK smallholding communities, magazines and YouTubers. ChatGPT-style answers commoditise basic Q&A, leaving premium value only in trusted human expertise.
scores.one_line: This is well-documented first-hand (70% of income from courses and membership), but it relies on the founder's expertise and support time, which Ricardo lacks and agents can't safely replace.

acquisition.why: Ranking in app stores for a clone is hard. Here traction came from a creator's audience, which carries partnership and platform dependence.

onboarding.why: App-store install and in-app signup run unattended.

delivery.why: Software wrapping AI APIs, with some monitoring for model and API cost drift.

billing.why: App-store or Stripe subscriptions are automated.

support.why: Agents can handle FAQs and refunds. App-review issues need a human.

scores.R_why: Ricardo could build it cheaply with AI app builders. The first-hand outcome was 1M+ views but only $35 revenue, and he has no creator distribution. UK GDPR and app-store compliance are manageable.
scores.M_why: Generic AI app clones are flooding app stores in 2026. Apple and Google clamp down on copycat apps, and the base AI models keep absorbing these features.
scores.one_line: The evidence is first-hand and negative: a low-value clone sold to a low-intent audience converted 1M views into $35, a clear cautionary tale rather than a model to copy.

acquisition.why: B2B cold email to UK listed companies (IR and CFO teams) is legal. Enterprise sales cycles, procurement and trust-building still need human calls and demos.

onboarding.why: Security reviews, NDAs, handling of market-sensitive pre-results data and integrations need human work.

delivery.why: The pipeline drafts scripts from filings and transcripts. Human executive review is mandatory, and the vendor carries accuracy liability.

billing.why: Enterprise invoices and purchase orders, partly automatable.

support.why: High-stakes clients expect responsive human support around results dates.

scores.R_why: Selling to listed companies requires credibility, insurance and infosec, and the product handles inside information under UK MAR and FCA rules [E]. UK reporting is half-yearly, with different filing sources from the US 10-K/10-Q. Unrealistic on 6-8 h/week and £300.
scores.M_why: IR-platform incumbents and AI research tools are adding earnings-prep features, and in-house Copilot or ChatGPT use substitutes cheaply [E]. Trust barriers favour established vendors.
scores.one_line: A 12-hour prototype with no buyer and a hypothetical time saving; enterprise sales and inside-information risk make it a poor fit for a solo, agent-run test.

acquisition.why: Podcast, YouTube and content are inbound and legal. Conversion depends on the coach's personal reputation and referrals, which agents can't fabricate.

onboarding.why: Booking, intake forms and contracts can be automated. Discovery calls are human.

delivery.why: One-to-one coaching, retreats and sessions are the coach's own time every time.

billing.why: Package payments via Stripe are automated.

support.why: Relationship-based. Clients expect the coach personally.

scores.R_why: Ricardo is not a coach and lacks an executive network or credentials. Delivery would consume all his hours. Hormone or health coaching in the UK risks straying into medical advice and ASA health-claim rules.
scores.M_why: The coaching market is very crowded and AI coaching apps are eroding the low end. Only differentiated, reputation-led coaches hold pricing.
scores.one_line: Revenue is never stated and the only first-hand claim is the coach's VC background; this is pure human-time services, the opposite of an agent-run business.
